name: ECG: what it records and what it can show
summary: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity through patches on the skin. This guide covers the test, longer recordings, what it shows and its limits.
keyPoints: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, including its rate and rhythm.
A standard ECG is quick and painless, and patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest.
A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording, which is why longer monitoring is sometimes used.
An ECG can help doctors tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past.

body.heading: What does an ECG record?
body.body: An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the electrical activity of the heart. The British Heart Foundation describes it as a simple test that records the heart's rhythm, its rate and its electrical activity. Each heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal, and the machine picks these signals up through sensors on the skin. The result is a graph of the signals.

body.heading: What happens during a standard ECG?
body.body: Sticky patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest and connected to the machine. The British Heart Foundation describes the test as quick and painless. The NHS puts a standard ECG at about 5 minutes. People are asked to lie still because movement can affect the recording.

body.heading: What can an ECG show?
body.body: The British Heart Foundation says an ECG can help doctors to tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past. The NHS says an ECG is usually done when a doctor suspects symptoms of a heart attack, coronary heart disease or an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia).

body.heading: What are the limits of a standard ECG?
body.body: A standard ECG captures only what happens while it is recording. A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording. That is why longer recordings or other heart tests are sometimes arranged.

body.heading: What are longer and exercise ECGs?
body.body: An ambulatory ECG, sometimes called Holter monitoring, records the heart's electrical activity continuously while the person goes about daily life. The NHS says people are usually asked to wear it for 24 to 48 hours, but it can be up to 7 days. It is used to look for heart rhythm problems that a short recording may miss. An exercise ECG monitors the heart while the person exercises and the heart is working harder. The British Heart Foundation describes an exercise ECG as an ECG recorded while the person walks on a treadmill or cycles, used to see how the heart behaves under exertion and to look for coronary heart disease. Doctors may suggest it for symptoms such as dizzy spells or blackouts. It is also used after procedures such as angioplasty, and to help set exercise levels for cardiac rehabilitation. The person walks or cycles at a gentle pace that gradually gets harder, and staff watch closely.

body.heading: How do the results reach the person?
body.body: The NHS says people may need a follow-up appointment to talk about their ECG results. The NHS says ECG results may be available on the same day, but can take a few weeks depending on the type of ECG. The British Heart Foundation says to call 999 immediately for signs of a heart attack, such as sudden chest pain that does not ease after a few minutes of rest.
